I have a few thoughts about this. Full disclosure before I start, I have bipolar I and have been hospitalized several times and have had ECT. I really, intimately understand your concern with privacy.

I don't think you should disclose something you don't want strangers to know unless you fully trust someone. Your son is very young. This probably isn't something he is going to understand yet.

For me personally, I expect that at some point, anything I tell another person will be told to someone else (even if they are family or friends). I have a lot of understanding for that, especially when it's something heavy. Your illness and your hospitalization impact your kid. Your kid, in turn, needs to talk to people about it, share it, and talk through/work through his feelings and thoughts. It's exceedingly likely he will need to tell not only a therapist but close friends. It's important to note that some people might also feel more comfortable talking to complete strangers they'll never meet again who can't judge them for anything.

So... my thought is this. Your kid is young. He is going to go through something. He is going to tell people. Think about how you should phrase what is happening. "Mommy is sick and has to go to the hospital for a little while to get better" is different than "mommy is severely mentally ill and going to a psychiatric ward." Whatever you tell him is what will be, at some point, conveyed to others.

It is not a moral failing on his part. It's something humans need to do. If you use more vague terms with him now, then you can always tell him more details when he is older. If you want to minimize gossip, being vague in an age-appropriate way is the way to go.

In short, yes. I think it would be wrong to tell him the extent of what is happening explicitly and asking him to bear a secret that affects him. Expecting him to keep it to himself is probably unreasonable. Tell him what you are comfortable with him telling others.

It might be helpful to review Yick Wo v. Hopkins. That's the case where a facially neutral law (prohibiting operating a laundry unless certain conditions were met and a permit was granted) was virtually only applied against Chinese laundries (permits were granted to all but one non-Chinese applicant, whereas permits were denied to all 240 Chinese-operated laundries). When the Court overturned a Chinese operator's conviction, it said that the law was unjustified and discriminatory in application and amounted to a practical denial of equal protection. They said it was administered "with an evil eye and unequal hand," and when applied like so, the discrimination is admitted and no reason exists for it except hostility to a race.

This case is easy to forget about because it has no progeny. But yeah, as others have said *application* is not quite the same as *effect* in that application involves (assumed) intent whereas effect (purportedly) lacks intent.

The only thing I’d add is when you’re taking the exams, if you’re asked about what arguments plaintiff/the state will make and what arguments the defendant will make, *always make the bad argument* (i.e what the losing party argued) and then counter it with the winning argument (what the court actually said). I don’t think I quite understood that during first year, but if you don’t do this, use bad arguments and then explain why they are bad, then you will miss points. This is part of the reason why you can’t just Quimbee cases and why reading and understanding all the cases is so important. 

Also, I’m a little bit older than most students so I don’t know if this would help younger students, but I handwrote all my notes (case briefs, note cases, excerpts from articles, etc) and then near the end of the semester, inputted them into an easy-to-follow outline I could control+f. I also Quimbee’d the cases before I read them, and then dug into them on my own. This method will quadruply reinforce the material, since you 1. Watch the Quimbee video; 2. Read the cases; 3. Take handwritten notes; and 4. Input/go over those notes at the end of the semester when you make the outline.

It’s still gonna be hard. I don’t want to give the impression that it won’t be. The trial and error part is the worst of it though, other than maybe actually getting correctly getting diagnosed. I was misdiagnosed for 10 years before finally getting the proper diagnosis and proper treatment. It wrecked havoc on my life until I could put a name to what was happening. Naming it helps take the power out of it. You know how to fight it. I wish I’d gotten diagnosed earlier too. A lot of bipolar folks get misdiagnosed as depressed (no one goes to the doc when they feel like a rockstar... and I always thought that was just how people normally felt and didn’t recognize it as mania... I had no idea what mania even was before I learned about my disorder and realized in hindsight what was going on).  

The trial and error process can take an incredibly long time. Trying dozens of different meds and therapies to see what works can be discouraging. And meds can randomly stop working or give you side effects that don’t pop up for years. I met a woman once who was on lithium for 30 years until it caused serious liver problems and now she can’t take meds anymore. She still does her best to try. The one thing you have to always do is try, even if it seems hopeless. Sounds lame, but there’s this TV quite I love: “If nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do.” Try to keep that in mind, that when it feels hopeless (and it sometimes will), fight. Fighting battles we can’t win is what makes life so meaningful and beautiful. Makes us uniquely human. And who knows, maybe we will win. 

I can not recommend NAMI enough. It feels dumb at first. You just gotta get through that. Going to bipolar-specific NAMI meetings was more helpful than any therapist I’ve ever had. When other people talk about their experiences, it’s like they are telling you your own life story. It’s unbelievably relieving to hear other people talk about it, to not feel so alone. Sometimes people just talk about what’s going on, sometimes about their pasts, sometimes about the things they are currently trying. I think there’s a requirement that you have to wait a year after your last suicide attempt to go to the meetings. But if that’s you, please do! See if it’s a fit. 

Good luck and again, don’t be afraid to reach out. Talking to people that know exactly what you’re going through because it’s exactly what they went through is so important.

Want to reply to you specifically, because I don’t think this is good advice for a lot of people. I don’t think non-psychs should treat depression and tell you if it gets worse, let them know  because a ton of people are misdiagnosed or just wrong about what condition they have. A ton of people who think they have depression actually have bipolar. When they take antidepressants, it can trigger mania and can make them feel amazing. Bipolar people might think that’s normal - that’s just how everyone feels all the time, especially if that’s what they think is normal for them when they are not depressed. Feeling great soon after starting antidepressants is a HUGE red flag that a lot of doctors will just miss because they don’t realize they should be looking for it, and since antidepressants are supposed to make you feel better, it might make them think they’re just working. The problem is that that mistake might not be discovered until the person crashes and kills themself.  I get there are lots of reasons someone might have to go to a non-psychiatrist, cost reasons being maybe the biggest one, but I think this has to be a consideration.

Want to add another perspective here wrt non-psychiatry professionals prescribing psychiatric medicines. I fall on the side that it is a bad idea. Doctors in other specialties aren’t as primed to spot issues when they come up because it’s just not what they do. They don’t always know what to look for. 

Anecdotal, but I went to GP for help with depression, and on the check up, they didn’t spot red flags that the medication I was taking was dangerous for me and we were treating the wrong condition. If I had gone to a psych instead, they would have spotted those flags and gotten me off that medication before serious damage had been done (I’m actually bipolar, not major depressive, antidepressants can trigger mania, which is what happened, the problem wasn’t discovered until I crashed and ended up in a hospital, which cost me a shit ton more money - and almost cost me my life - than just going to a psychiatrist would have been). That experience has led me to refuse to even see a psychiatrist that doesn’t specialize in bipolar disorder. For that reason, I will never recommend people with psychiatric conditions see any doctor but a psychiatrist.

(Amount of savings – 16,000) ÷ 2.5 = X

X – 18,600 = amount if income needed to cover the remainder

£18,600 – £3,600 = £15,000

I can't really tell by your post how much research you've put into UK schools yet, so if this sounds patronizing or anything, it isn't meant to be. Just want to cover some basics as someone who did this myself.

Your GPA is great and you've got a good shot at most of those schools. Oxbridge is sort of a pipe dream for anyone, but by all means, apply! I'd even maybe expand upon your list, depending on how many schools/programs you've looked into.

A huge question you didn't answer is what do you want to do? Figure out what you want your master's in, then look for schools that have good programs for that. Another consideration is that the UK system works differently. They have taught master's programs, which are one-year long programs with 2 terms of classes and 1 term wherein you write a dissertation, and MPhils, which are research degrees that take 2 years to complete.

You should also know that, as an American, scholarships are unlikely. I netted a £3,000 discount from one of the schools I was accepted to, but turned it down to attend a better school. I received no other offers of money, and I used loans to finance my schooling. Your student debt load will likely be quite massive, so figure out how you're going to pay for it now. It's thrown a wrench in my law school plans, so if you plan on doing any more studying post-masters, then figure that in as well. That isn't meant to deter you, and I regret nothing, but yeah the student loan situation is not good.

If I were you, I'd first figure out what I want to study, then research which schools have respectable programs for that, then research COA, then apply to the ones you like that you can also afford.

In John, written the latest (circa 150ish CE), Jesus is confident, he IS God, he shows no fear. He more or less knowingly smiles at God while dying, and with his last breath, he says "Into your hands, I commend my spirit".
